title: Observability Toolkit for Model Rollouts: per-route diffs, traces & auto-rollback UX
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Problem: Teams deploying model variants (canaries, A/B, and shadow traffic) lack a unified Console view that shows per-route performance, request-level traces, and cohort diffs that reliably surface regressions. Without that visibility it takes manual sampling and spreadsheets to decide whether to promote or rollback a variant.

Goal: Add an observability toolkit in Console that makes rollout decisions fast and safe. The toolkit will include per-route metric breakdowns (latency p50/p95, token cost, error rate), side-by-side cohort diff views (relative and absolute), sampled request traces linked to diffs, built-in shadow-traffic comparison, and a configurable auto-rollback policy UI with audit logging and human override. The feature should integrate with existing runtime tagging and the telemetry pipeline so product engineers can run canary and A/B experiments with clear SLOs and automated safety nets.
acceptance_criteria: Console has a new 'Rollout Observability' panel available under each route with a cohort selector (control/canary/variants)
Per-route metrics are shown for selectable windows (1h/6h/24h) and include latency p50/p95, error rate, token usage, and cost per 1k tokens
Cohort diff view shows both absolute delta and percentage change for each metric and highlights deviations beyond configured thresholds
Traces: a sampled set of request traces are linkable from the diff rows and include request prompt, model variant, response tokens, and error stack if present
Shadow traffic support: side-by-side comparison of production vs shadowed variant with clear labeling and no traffic impact on responses
Auto-rollback: UI to configure simple rollback policies (e.g., rollback if error_rate_up > 2x AND p95_latency_up > 200ms for 10m) and a simulation mode to preview actions
Audit logs and rollout timeline visible in Console with who/when actions (rollout start, traffic shift, rollback) and links to relevant PRs/dashboards
Backend telemetry endpoints and query performance meet SLOs (diff query typical latency < 600ms for 24h window on medium routes)
Design review completed and security/data review signed off before shipping to Dedicated/Private customers
implementation_notes: Backend: extend metrics API to support cohort-level aggregations and delta computations; prefer query-time diffing to avoid duplication but add caching for frequent queries
Storage: short-term high-cardinality metrics retention (24-72h) for rollout diffs, with long-term rollup metrics stored in existing TSDB
Tracing: require runtime to tag requests with rollout_id and cohort_name (ENG-5021), sampling at 1% by default with ability to increase for canaries
Auto-rollback: implement policy engine as part of rollout service with idempotent actions and human-confirm fallback; integrate with rollout API to perform traffic shifts and rollback calls to router
UI: cohort selector, diff table with sortable metrics, sparkline per metric, expandable row to show example traces, timeline widget for traffic shifts
Default threshold presets: performance-safe, conservative, and aggressive; offer JSON editor for advanced policies
Privacy: scrub PII from stored traces and mask tokens; follow Private deployment KMS/audit guidelines
open_decisions: Compute diffs at query time vs precompute and store snapshots: tradeoff between storage cost and faster UI responsiveness
Default window for diffs (24h recommended) and whether to show adaptive baselines (rolling vs fixed pre-rollout baseline)
What quality metrics to surface by default beyond latency/error/cost (e.g., hallucination score, semantic similarity) given computing cost
Retention policy for sampled traces in Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (shorter retention in Hosted to reduce cost)
tradeoffs: Precomputing diffs reduces UI latency but increases storage and ingest complexity; query-time diffs simplify ingestion but require efficient TSDB queries
Higher trace sampling gives clearer debugging signals but increases storage and may expose sensitive prompt content unless redacted
Rich default metrics help most customers but increase backend CPU and complexity—start with a core set and make others opt-in
Auto-rollback must balance safety vs noise; conservative defaults reduce false rollbacks but may delay mitigation
